summary: Children solve elapsed-time word problems in both directions — finding the END time from a start and a duration, and finding the DURATION between two times — using a blank number line and counting on in convenient jumps (to the next o'clock, then whole hours, then minutes). The core teaching move is showing that the SAME number line solves both 'when does it end?' and 'how long is it?', so elapsed time becomes one count-on method rather than two mysterious sums. Persistent errors to target: treating time as base-10 by writing minutes past 60 without rolling the hour over (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62'), column subtraction that fails across the hour boundary, and counting in the wrong direction.
misconceptions: Adds the duration to the minutes only, ignoring the hour roll-over past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62')
Column subtraction of the two times, failing across the hour boundary
Counts in the wrong direction (subtracts a duration instead of adding, or vice versa)
Overshoots or undershoots the o'clock bridge (base-10 slip)

activities.title: Count on along a number line to find the end time
steps: Read a word problem such as: 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?'
Draw a blank number line and mark the start time (2:15).
Make a first jump that bridges to the next o'clock: +45 minutes to reach 3:00.
Make a second jump with the remaining minutes: +2 to reach 3:02; label each jump and read off the end time.
Repeat with a harder bridge: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Jump +20 to 4:00, then +15 to reach 4:15.
Check the end time on a clock face.
activities.insight: Adding a duration means counting FORWARD from the start; bridging to the next o'clock first makes the hour roll over correctly, so you never write an impossible time like 2:62 or 3:75.

activities.title: Fill the gap to find a duration
steps: Read a problem such as: 'How many minutes are there between 9:20 and 10:05?'
On a blank number line, mark both times (9:20 and 10:05).
Jump from the earlier time to the next o'clock: +40 minutes to reach 10:00.
Jump the remaining minutes: +5 to reach 10:05.
Add the jumps together (40 + 5) to get the total duration of 45 minutes.
Check against a clock face, and explain why adding 9:20 and 10:05 together would be nonsense.
activities.insight: Finding a duration means filling the GAP between two times with jumps and summing them — not subtracting in columns and not adding the two clock times together. Bridging the o'clock keeps the base-60 boundary correct.

activities.title: Decide the direction before you jump
steps: Before calculating any problem, state out loud whether the unknown is an END time (jump forward from the start by the duration), a START time (jump backward from the end by the duration) or a GAP (fill the space between two given times).
Solve a mixed set, e.g. 'A show ends at 10:05 and lasted 45 minutes — when did it START?' by counting BACKWARD: -5 to 10:00, then -40 to 9:20.
Compare a forward problem and a backward problem side by side, labelling which way the jumps go.
Say which number is unknown and which direction the jumps travel before marking the line.
activities.insight: Choosing the direction first — forward to find an end, backward to find a start, or filling the gap to find a duration — prevents counting the wrong way or adding two clock times together.

checkQuestion: Set both problem types and WATCH: (1) 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end? Show me your jumps.' (2) 'How many minutes between 9:20 and 10:05?' (3) A crossing-the-hour end-time: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Watch whether they count on with a number line (bridging the o'clock) or add minutes past 60, subtract in columns, or go the wrong direction.
checkAnswer: For the film, counts on 2:15 to 3:00 (+45) then +2 = 3:02 (or +47 bridging correctly); for 9:20 to 10:05 counts +40 to 10:00, +5 = 45 minutes; for 3:40 + 35 bridges to 4:00 (+20), +15 = 4:15 — rolling the hour over rather than writing 3:75.
